options.text: The chest cavity containing the breathing structures
options.explanation: That is the named region of the respiratory system.
The abdomen sits below the diaphragm.
The trachea is inside the thorax, not the thorax.
That is the alveoli.

questions.stem: Which is the correct airway order during inhalation?

options.explanation: The alveoli are the destination, not a waypoint.
Air travels from wide to fine to the sacs.
Bronchioles come after the bronchi.
The trachea comes first.

questions.stem: What do the pleural membranes do?

options.explanation: Voicing is the larynx's business.
Filtering happens in the upper airways.

options.text: They wrap around the lungs and coat the thorax's inner lining
options.explanation: Those thin layers wrap and line.
Exchange belongs to the alveoli.

questions.stem: How many bronchi does a human have?

options.explanation: Each lung gets its own bronchus.
Hundreds describes bronchioles, not bronchi.

options.text: None — air reaches the lungs directly
options.explanation: The bronchi are the connection.
The trachea splits into exactly two.

questions.stem: Which structure is described as the specialised gas exchange surface?

options.explanation: Exchange happens at those sacs.
The trachea conducts air; it does not exchange.
They distribute air; exchange happens downstream.
They line and lubricate, not exchange.

questions.stem: List the contents of the thorax named in the specification.
questions.modelAnswer: Ribs, intercostal muscles, diaphragm, trachea, lungs with their bronchi, bronchioles and alveoli, and the pleural membranes.

questions.stem: Give the singular forms of bronchi and alveoli.
Explain why the airway's branching order matters to know.
questions.modelAnswer: Because questions hand you diagrams or ask for sequences, and the route is strictly one-way: trachea to bronchus to bronchiole to alveolus; swapping bronchi and bronchioles reverses the widening-narrowing logic and loses the marks.

questions.stem: A diagram shows a branching tree ending in clustered sacs, with muscle bands between curved bones around it. Label five structures and one function each.
questions.modelAnswer: Ribs — protection; intercostal muscles — moving the ribs; trachea — air's main road; bronchioles — distribution within the lung; alveoli — the gas exchange surface; with the diaphragm resizing the floor beneath.

questions.stem: What provides the lungs' large surface area?

options.explanation: Ribs protect; they do not exchange.
Area comes from sheer numbers of sacs.
The trachea conducts; it contributes no exchange area.
They line the cavity, not exchange.

questions.stem: How thick are the alveolar and capillary walls?

options.explanation: Each wall is one cell; the pair adds up to two.
Wall thickness is fixed anatomy.
The double barrier stays minimal.
Much thicker walls would slow exchange badly.

questions.stem: What keeps oxygen levels high in the alveolar air?

options.explanation: Moisture helps dissolving, not renewal.
Thinness shortens the path; it does not renew the air.
Blood renews its own side; ventilation handles the air side.

options.text: Ventilation — the constant renewal of air by breathing
options.explanation: Fresh breaths replace the used air.

questions.stem: What does a good blood supply maintain?

options.text: Steep concentration gradients by renewing the blood side
options.explanation: Fresh arrivals keep the capillary side imbalanced.

options.text: The strength of the rib cage
options.explanation: Ribs need no blood supply for this purpose.
Bronchiole width is not blood-dependent.
Moisture is a local film, not a blood task.

questions.stem: Why do breathing rate and heart rate rise together in exercise?

options.explanation: Distinct muscles drive each.

options.text: Because both are renewal pumps for the same gradients that exercise is draining
options.explanation: Air side and blood side renew faster together.

options.text: Because the body needs less oxygen
options.explanation: Exercise needs more.
No new alveoli appear.

questions.stem: Name the four shared adaptations of exchange surfaces.
questions.modelAnswer: Large surface area, thin walls, good ventilation and a good blood supply.

questions.stem: Which two structures are one cell thick at the exchange site?
questions.modelAnswer: The alveolus wall and the capillary wall.

questions.stem: Explain why a collapsed lung's region exchanges poorly even if its blood supply survives.
questions.modelAnswer: Because without ventilation the air side never renews: oxygen falls and carbon dioxide rises until the alveolar air matches the blood, the gradients vanish, and diffusion stalls however good the circulation remains.

questions.stem: At altitude, both breathing rate and heart rate climb even at rest. Use the four adaptations to explain the body's strategy.
questions.modelAnswer: Thinner air lowers the oxygen side of every gradient, so the body raises the renewal rates: faster breathing refreshes the alveolar air more often and a faster heart delivers blood through the one-cell-thick walls more frequently, compensating for the smaller per-breath oxygen with more exchanges per minute across the unchanged large surface area.
